chapter: Last years of the band and reflections
title: 1947: Jimmy Forrest, Ernie Wilkins and the Tunetown Ballroom closure
summary: The band works the Tunetown Ballroom with Jimmy Forrest, Ernie Wilkins and Betty Roche until the IRS closes it, owing them about $800 they never recover.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: But that 1945 trip there was a great trip. The band didn't do so hot in '46. But the band went back in '47, that's when we had Jimmy Forrest with us. We played that (musical sounds), remember that song? ("Sunrise Serenade"-ed.)

John Cotter made the arrangements for us, and Jimmy Forrest and Lucille Agers really broke it up. On that particular trip. But '46 we came back to St. Louis. The music started going, the big bands started getting farther away. Started getting rough. We would get a few gigs here and there, a few gigs here and there.

Then we started working in '47. We would work in the Tunetown Ballroom maybe two or three times a week. And the last date we had at the Tunetown Ballroom was the last night the Tunetown Ballroom was open. The Internal Revenue men came in, and closed the Tunetown Ballroom down. They owed us about $800- some. Which was a lot of money back at that time. We never got
a penny of our money. We had Ernie Wilkins and his brother playing in the band at this time. Ernie was writing real nice, was writing real good.
We had Betty Roche who was a singer.

I think we had the biggest band of our career. We had at the Tunetown Ballroom. And when that job fell through, by the Ballroom closing, and they auctioned off the stuff, we didn't know, but we could have applied --

Put a lien on it and gotten our salary out of what they sold. You know what I mean? Because we had first preference. But we didn't know that. And they don't tell you these things. You wake up five, six years later and you realize what you could have done, had you known.
